LESSONS.title: Tuples
LESSONS.goal: Make an unchangeable bundle (a tuple) and take values out
summary: A tuple is values wrapped in ( )
Take values out by index; no changing
One value needs a comma: (5,)

cards.say: A tuple is a bundle of values wrapped in parentheses. You take values out by index, just like a list, but once it's made, it can't change. It's perfect for fixed bundles like coordinates.
Try to change a value and you get a TypeError clue. Also, a tuple with just one value needs a comma, like (5,). (5) is just a number wearing parentheses.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Indexes start at 0, so p[1] is the second value, 7. Tuples use indexes just like lists.

items.q: What's the output of this code?
items.explain: A tuple can't change after it's made. p[0] = 9 gives a TypeError clue, and the code never reaches print.

items.q: Fill in the blank to make a tuple with one value.
items.explain: A comma, as in (5,), makes it a tuple. Without the comma it's just a number, and a dot would make a float like 5.0.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: len counts the values in the tuple. There are three, so it's 3.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print a point and then its first value.
items.explain: Make the tuple first, print the whole thing, then take out the first value and print it. Using it before it exists is a NameError.

items.task: Read x and y with input(), one after the other (leave the parentheses empty), and turn them into int. Make a tuple p = (x, y), print p, then print p[0] + p[1] on the next line. Example: input 3, 5 → (3, 5) then 8
hints: You print two lines: the tuple as it is, then the sum of its two values. Look at what happens to 3 and 5 in the example.
A tuple wraps values in parentheses, separated by commas. To take one out, use an index, like with a list.
Put a tuple of x and y into p. For the sum, take out p's first and second values by index and add them.

x = int(input())
y = int(input())
p = (___, ___)
print(p)
print(p[0] + p[___])
items.solution:
x = int(input())
y = int(input())
p = (x, y)
print(p)
print(p[0] + p[1])
items.explain: Printing the tuple (x, y) shows it in parentheses, and indexes 0 and 1 take out each value. It works the same with negatives and zeros.

items.q: Which statement about tuples is true?
options: Its values can't change after it's made
It can only be made with square brackets
items.explain: A tuple is a bundle that can't change. You make it with parentheses, and trying to change a value gives a TypeError clue.

LESSONS.title: Pack and unpack
LESSONS.goal: Unpack several values at once and return them from a function
summary: a, b = 1, 2 stores both at once
a, b = b, a swaps two values
return a, b gives back a tuple

cards.say: Separate names with commas and you can unpack several values onto several labels at once. To swap two values, a, b = b, a is all it takes. No temporary variable needed!
cards.code:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

cards.say: A function can return several values too: just put commas after return. The caller unpacks them. The number of labels must match the number of values.
cards.code:
def two(n):
    return n - 1, n + 1

lo, hi = two(5)
print(lo, hi)

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
a = 10
b = 20
a, b = b, a
print(a)
items.explain: a, b = b, a swaps the two values, so a now holds 20.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 3 is unpacked into x and 4 into y. Adding two numbers gives 7.

items.q: Fill in the blank to return the smallest and the largest together.
items.code:
def span(a, b, c):
    return min(a, b, c), ___

lo, hi = span(9, 3, 5)
print(lo, hi)
items.explain: Return min and max separated by a comma, and the two values unpack into lo and hi. The max chip prints the function itself, and the a, b, c chip makes four values: ValueError (too many values to unpack).

items.q: What's the output of this code?
items.explain: There are three values but only two labels, so you get a ValueError clue. The counts must match.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print 4 and then 8.
items.explain: Define the function first, call it and unpack into a and b, then print. a is 4 and b is 8.

items.task: Read three integers with input(), one after another (leave the parentheses empty). Write a function min_max(a, b, c) that returns the smallest and largest together, unpack them into lo, hi, and print(lo, hi). Example: input 3, 9, 5 → 3 9
items.starter:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
hints: You print two values on one line: the smallest and the largest. What happens if all three numbers are the same?
A function can return two values if you separate them with a comma after return. The caller also writes two labels with a comma.
Use min and max inside the function, and unpack the result of the call into lo and hi. You can define the function before reading the input.

def min_max(a, b, c):
    return ___, ___

a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
lo, hi = min_max(a, b, c)
print(lo, hi)
items.solution:
def min_max(a, b, c):
    return min(a, b, c), max(a, b, c)

a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
lo, hi = min_max(a, b, c)
print(lo, hi)
items.explain: return min(...), max(...) comes back as one tuple, and lo, hi = unpacks it. Even when all three are equal, it prints 7 7 just fine.

items.q: What does a, b = b, a do?
options: Swaps the values of the two labels
Checks whether a and b are equal
items.explain: The b, a on the right is bundled first, then unpacked into a, b, so the values trade places.

LESSONS.title: items and sorting
LESSONS.goal: Use items() and sorted to rank by value
summary: d.items() gives (key, value) tuples
sorted(…, key=function) sets the rule
Biggest first: reverse=True

cards.say: items() hands out (key, value) tuples. Remember for name, value in d.items()? It was unpacking exactly these tuples. Wrap it in list() to see their shape.

Pass a function name to key=, without parentheses. sorted calls that function on each item and ranks by what it returns. reverse=True puts the biggest first. A trailing comma before the closing ) is fine too.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: items() gives tuples in (key, value) order. The key 'a' comes first, the value 3 second.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: This is why the key function used pair[1]: it takes out the tuple's second value, the count.

items.q: Fill in the blank to rank from the smallest value.
items.explain: Pass only the function name to key, no parentheses. get_n(p) and p[1] are a NameError here, because there's no p at this spot.

items.q: What do you add to sorted to rank the biggest first?
items.explain: Add reverse=True and the order flips, so the biggest comes first.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print each key and value on its own line.
items.explain: Make the dictionary first, then unpack (key, value) and print inside the loop. "Done" appears only once, after the loop ends.

items.task: Read the sales counts of coffee, tea and juice with input(), one after another (leave the parentheses empty), and turn them into int. Make a sales dictionary, sort it with a def function as key, and print “name count” per line, best seller first. Example: input 5, 9, 2 → tea 9 / coffee 5 / juice 2
items.starter:
c = int(input())
t = int(input())
j = int(input())
sales = {"coffee": c, "tea": t,
         "juice": j}
hints: Print one line per menu item as “name count”, best seller first. Look at the example: how did 9, 5, 2 come out?
items() gives (key, value) tuples. Pass a function to sorted's key and it ranks by what that function returns.
Write a small function that returns the tuple's second value, pass it as key, and add the option for biggest first. Unpack the result with for and print.
items.solution:
c = int(input())
t = int(input())
j = int(input())
sales = {"coffee": c, "tea": t,
         "juice": j}

def get_count(pair):
    return pair[1]

rank = sorted(
    sales.items(),
    key=get_count,
    reverse=True,
)
for name, n in rank:
    print(name, n)
items.explain: get_count returns the tuple's second value, and key plus reverse=True ranks the best seller first. A menu item that sold 0 lands neatly at the end.

items.q: What does each item from items() look like?
items.explain: It's a tuple pairing a key with its value. That's why you can unpack it, as in for k, v in d.items().

LESSONS.title: Sets
LESSONS.goal: Use sets to remove duplicates and find common values
summary: A set has no duplicates, no order
& common, | combined, - left over
An empty set is set(); {} is an empty dictionary
add puts a value in; in checks for it

cards.say: A set gathers values with no duplicates. Just write values inside curly braces. It has no order, so you can't take values out by index; use sorted() to print it neatly.
& is what's common, | combines, and - is what's left after subtracting. An empty set is set(), not {}, because {} is an empty dictionary. Wrap a list in set() and duplicates disappear.
Add to a set one value at a time with add. Add a value that's already there and it still stays as one. Check membership with value in set. Start an empty set with set().
cards.code:
seen = set()
seen.add("Ria")
seen.add("Ria")
print(len(seen), "Ria" in seen)

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The repeated 1 stays only once, giving {1, 2}, so the count is 2.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: & keeps only values found in both sets. The only value they share is 3.

items.q: Fill in the blank to print the union [1, 2, 3].
items.explain: | combines two sets. & gives the common [2], and - gives a minus b, which is [1].

items.q: What's the right way to make an empty set?
items.explain: {} is an empty dictionary and [] is an empty list. An empty set can only be made with set().

items.q: Put the lines in order to print the count without duplicates.
items.explain: Make the list, remove duplicates with set(), then print the count. a appears twice but counts once, so it's 2.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
s = set()
s.add(3)
s.add(3)
s.add(5)
print(len(s))
items.explain: 3 stays as one even though it was added twice, and 5 is added, so there are 2 values.

items.q: Fill in the blank to print True.
items.explain: Jun was never added, so not in is True. in gives False, and == compares a set with a string, which is False.

items.task: Read two classes' clubs with input(), one line each (leave the parentheses empty). Names are separated by spaces. split() each, turn them into set(), find the common clubs with &, and print(sorted(...)). Example: “chess reading” and “reading cooking” → ['reading']

tests.stdin:
chess soccer reading
reading cooking chess

hints: Print only the clubs both classes have, as an alphabetical list. What would print if nothing overlaps?
split() breaks a string into a list. Wrap it in set() and duplicates vanish, and sets have a symbol for finding what's common.
Turn each line's split() list into a set() to get two sets. The common result has no order, so print it with sorted.

a = set(input().split())
b = set(___)
print(sorted(a ___ b))
items.solution:
a = set(input().split())
b = set(input().split())
print(sorted(a & b))
items.explain: set() removed the duplicates and & kept only the common ones. A set has no order, so print it with sorted to get the same result every time. If nothing overlaps, you get an empty list [].

items.q: What happens if the same value goes into a set twice?
items.explain: Sets don't allow duplicates. Equal values merge into one.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 9 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Use tuples, unpacking, items sorting and sets
summary: Tuples can't change; one value: (5,)
a, b = b, a and returning many values
items + key sorting, sets & | -

cards.say: Chapter 9 checkpoint! A tuple is a bundle that can't change, and commas let you unpack it. Sets remove duplicates, so set() plus sorted() can tidy up a word list nicely.

items.q: What's the output of this code?
items.explain: Tuples can't change, so t[0] = 5 gives a TypeError clue.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: (7) is an integer and (7,) is a tuple, so their types differ. A one-value tuple needs the comma.

items.q: Fill in the blank to swap the values of x and y.
items.code:
x = 1
y = 2
x, y = ___
print(x, y)
items.explain: x, y = y, x swaps the values and prints 2 1. x, x makes both 1, and a single y can't be unpacked, so it's a TypeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print 4.
items.explain: Define the function, call it and unpack into lo, hi, then print hi. pair(3) returns (3, 4).

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The second item of items() is the tuple with key 'b' and value 2.

items.q: Fill in the blank to rank from the smallest value.
items.explain: Pass only the function name to key, no parentheses. Ranked by value, you get [('b', 1), ('a', 3)].

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The set removes the duplicate, leaving {1, 3}, and sorted turns it into a list from smallest up.

items.task: Tidying a vocabulary list. Read the words on one line with input(), separated by spaces (leave the parentheses empty). Remove duplicates with set(), print the count with len, then print the sorted list on the next line. Example: apple banana apple → 2, then ['apple', 'banana']
hints: You print two lines: first the number of different words, then an alphabetical list.
set() removes duplicates, and a set has no order, so use sorted when you print it as a list.
Turn the split() list into a set() stored in uniq, then print its count with len and its sorted list with sorted.

words = input().split()
uniq = set(___)
print(len(___))
print(sorted(___))
items.solution:
words = input().split()
uniq = set(words)
print(len(uniq))
print(sorted(uniq))
items.explain: You printed the count and the sorted list of uniq, which set() made duplicate-free. It works even with a single word or the same word repeated.

items.q: What does {} make?
items.explain: {} is an empty dictionary. An empty set is set(), and an empty tuple is ().

ADVANCED.title: Changing sort rules
ADVANCED.goal: Set a sort rule in one line with lambda
summary: lambda p: p[1] is a short nameless function
Write it right in sorted/sort's key=
Tuple key: ties go to the next value

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. A short function like get_count from 9-3 can be a one-line lambda right in the key spot. lambda p: p[1] takes p and returns p[1].
cards.code:
d = {"latte": 5, "mocha": 2, "tea": 8}

def get_count(pair):
    return pair[1]

a = sorted(d.items(), key=get_count)
b = sorted(
    d.items(), key=lambda p: p[1])
print(b)
print(a == b)

cards.say: .sort() takes key= too. If the key is a tuple, ties on the first value are broken by the next one. Put - in front of a number and bigger numbers come first.
cards.code:
ps = [("b", 5), ("a", 5), ("c", 9)]
ps.sort(
    key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))
print(ps)

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The key is p[1], the second value, so 1 comes before 3. The order of the first values, a and b, isn't looked at.

items.q: Fill in the blank to sort the words from shortest to longest.
items.explain: len(w) returns the number of characters. Plain len is the function itself, which can't be compared, so it's a TypeError, and w[1] is an IndexError on the one-letter d.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
ps = [("a", 3), ("b", 9)]
r = sorted(ps, key=lambda p: p[1],
           reverse=True)
print(r[0][0])
items.explain: With reverse=True, the big value 9 comes first. r[0] is ("b", 9), and its first value is b.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print one line per item, smallest value first.
items.explain: Make the list, sort it with a lambda as key, then unpack and print in a loop. b has the smaller second value, so it comes first.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The second values tie at 5, so the tuple key's next value, the name, decides. a comes before b, so a is first.

items.task: Read three menu items with input(), one “name price” per line (leave the parentheses empty). Using sorted and key=lambda, print “name price” per line, cheapest first, and by name when prices tie. Example: tea 3000 / latte 3000 / mocha 2000 → mocha 2000, latte 3000, tea 3000
items.starter:
items = []
for i in range(3):
    name, price = input().split()
    items.append((name, int(price)))
hints: Print three lines, cheapest first. Can you also spot in the example that equal prices go by name?
You can write a lambda right in key=. If the key is a tuple, ties on the first value are broken by the next one.
Each tuple in items is (name, price). Pass a lambda that returns a tuple with the price first and the name second.

rank = sorted(items,
    key=lambda p: (p[___], p[___]))
for name, price in rank:
    print(name, price)
items.solution:
items = []
for i in range(3):
    name, price = input().split()
    items.append((name, int(price)))

rank = sorted(
    items, key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0]))
for name, price in rank:
    print(name, price)
items.explain: key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0]) looks at the price first and the name on ties. Prices are ints, so 100, 20 and 3 line up by numeric size.

items.q: In key=lambda p: p[1], what does the lambda do?
options: Returns the value to rank each item by
items.explain: sorted calls the lambda on each item and ranks by what comes back. It does the same job as the def get_count function.

ADVANCED.title: Comparing sets
ADVANCED.goal: Compare sets with ^ and <=, and remove with discard
summary: a ^ b: values in only one side
a <= b: is all of a inside b?
discard removes, no error if missing

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. ^ joins 9-4's &, | and -. ^ gives values found in only one side, and <= asks “is the left side all inside the right?” == checks equality, ignoring order.
discard removes a value from a set. It's add's partner from 9-4. Discarding a value that isn't there just moves on, no error.
cards.code:
s = {1, 2, 3}
s.discard(2)
s.discard(9)
print(sorted(s))
print(1 in s, 2 in s)

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: ^ gives values in only one of the two. 2 and 3 are in both, so they drop out, leaving 1 and 4.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: <= is True if every value on the left is inside the right. Both 1 and 2 are on the right.

items.q: Fill in the blank to print [1, 4], the values in only one side.
items.explain: ^ gives values in only one side. & gives the common [2, 3], and | gives the combined [1, 2, 3, 4].

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: discard(1) removes 1. Discarding 5, which isn't there, moves on without an error.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print 2, then False on the next line.
items.explain: Make the set, remove 2, then print. Two values remain, so the length is 2, and 2 is gone now, so it's False.

items.task: Read yesterday's and today's attendees with input(), one line each (leave the parentheses empty; names are split by spaces), and make each a set(). Print sorted(...) of those who came only one day, using ^. Then print whether everyone today also came yesterday, using <=. Example: “Minji Jun Seo” and “Jun Hana” → ['Hana', 'Minji', 'Seo'] then False
hints: You print two lines: a list of people who came only one day, then True or False. What if both days are identical?
Sets have a symbol for values in only one side, and another for checking whether one is all inside the other.
Turn each line's split() list into a set(). Print the ^ result with sorted, then print today <= yesterday as is.

y = set(line1.split())
t = set(___)
print(sorted(y ___ t))
print(t ___ y)
items.solution:
line1 = input()
line2 = input()
y = set(line1.split())
t = set(line2.split())
print(sorted(y ^ t))
print(t <= y)
items.explain: y ^ t finds who came only one day, and t <= y checks whether everyone today also came yesterday. If both days match, you get [] and True.

items.q: What does it mean when a <= b is True?
options: All of a's values are inside b
a and b are exactly the same
items.explain: <= is a subset check. It's True when a equals b, and True when all of a fits inside b.

ADVANCED.title: No-repeat roll call
ADVANCED.goal: Tidy up an attendance list with sets and lambda sorting
summary: add and in spot first-timers
| combines; ^ gives who came only one week
Tuple key=lambda: short names first

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. With 9-4's add and in, you can spot who already came. A set counts the same name only once.
| gives everyone from both weeks, and ^ gives those who came only one week. Sort the names with key=lambda: shortest first, alphabetical on ties.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
seen = set()
for n in ["a", "b", "a"]:
    seen.add(n)
print(len(seen))
items.explain: a stays as one even though it was added twice, leaving a and b: 2 values.

items.q: Fill in the blank to print “Back again!”
items.explain: Ria is already in seen, so in is True. not in prints First time!, and == compares a string with a set, which is False, so it also prints First time!

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Fewest characters first, so Min leads, and the five-letter Doyun and Hayun go alphabetically. A plain sorted would put Doyun first.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: b is in both, so it drops out, leaving a and c: 2.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print 2, then Done on the next line.
items.explain: Make the list, remove duplicates with set(), then print the count. a appears twice but it's still 2, and Done comes last.

items.task: Read week 1 and week 2 attendance names with input(), one line each (leave the parentheses empty). Make a and b with split() and set(), print the combined count (|), then print those who came only one week (^), sorted with key=lambda: shortest name first, alphabetical on ties. Example: “Ria Min Ria” and “Min Hayun Yu” → 4 / ['Yu', 'Ria', 'Hayun']

tests.stdin:
Ria Min Ria
Min Hayun Yu

hints: You print two lines: the combined head count, then the list of people who came only one week. A name repeated on one line counts once.
set() removes duplicates, and sets have a symbol to combine and one for values in only one side. Set the sort rule with lambda.
split() each line and make sets a and b. Count from the union, and sort the one-side-only values with a (length, name) tuple key.

a = set(line1.split())
b = set(line2.split())
print(len(a ___ b))
print(sorted(a ___ b,
    key=lambda n: (___, n)))
items.solution:
line1 = input()
line2 = input()
a = set(line1.split())
b = set(line2.split())
print(len(a | b))
print(sorted(a ^ b,
    key=lambda n: (len(n), n)))
items.explain: a | b counts everyone without duplicates, and a ^ b is ranked by a (length, name) key. Identical weeks give [], and equal lengths go by name.

items.q: What order does key=lambda n: (len(n), n) give?
options: Shortest first, then by name on ties
By name, then by length on ties
items.explain: A tuple key compares from the front. Smaller len(n) comes first, and only on a tie does the name n decide.

TEMPLATES.q: The point is stored in a tuple. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: Tuple indexes start at 0 too, so p[1] is the second value. A tuple can't change, so p[1] = … causes an error.

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank to swap the two values so it prints {B} {A}.
TEMPLATES.explain: a, b = b, a swaps both values at once. With only a = b, just a changes and the same value prints twice.

TEMPLATES.q: Some customer numbers were written twice. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: set() merges repeated values into one. Counting only the different values → {OUT}

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank to print only the numbers in both classes.
TEMPLATES.explain: & keeps the values in both sides (the intersection). | combines everything, and - keeps only values in the first one.

TEMPLATES.q: The score table was sorted by name. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: items() returns (name, score) pairs, and sorted compares from the front, so they line up by name. sorted(sc) sorts only names, and values() only scores.
